title: Developing a methodology to assess liquid metal embrittlement impact on the fatigue life of resistance spot welds
abstract: Abstract Third-generation advanced high-strength steels (3G AHSS) are widely used in automotive applications due to their exceptional mechanical properties, including high tensile strength and fracture toughness. Resistance spot welding is the dominant joining process for these steels in the body-in-white production due to the high productivity and automation capability. Though exhibiting satisfying welding current ranges, AHSS can have the downside of showing zinc-induced liquid metal embrittlement (Zn-LME), a phenomenon in which the exposure of the susceptible base material to the liquid zinc coating in combination with the induced tensile stresses during resistance spot welding can lead to cracking of varying severity. The presence of zinc-induced LME cracks can result in an unexpected failure of the component due to potential premature crack initiation and propagation under a mechanical load. While extensive research has been conducted on the effects of LME on static mechanical properties such as tensile strength and fracture toughness, its impact on fatigue life—a critical factor in the automotive application—remains less well understood. Fatigue failure can occur earlier as the presence of LME can accelerate the crack growth under cyclic loading. Understanding the interplay between LME-induced cracks formed during resistance spot welding and fatigue behavior is essential for improving the reliability and widening the application field of 3G AHSS. This study, which is the first part of a larger investigation, is aimed at developing a methodology for analyzing the influence of zinc-induced LME on the fatigue life of third-generation advanced high-strength steels (3G AHSS), focusing on the fatigue crack initiation and propagation mechanism under cyclic loading. To achieve this, LME cracks were generated via the usage of a decreasing electrode force profile and the reproducibility was investigated. The LME crack surface was investigated with stereo and scanning electron microscopy. The fatigue test for a specimen with severe LME cracking was monitored via digital image correlation (DIC), which enabled the evaluation of critical areas. The derived methodology serves as a guideline for quantifying the influence on LME cracks on the fatigue life and thereby assisting the development process of new materials and parts. In upcoming investigations, the methodology will be used to evaluate the influence of specific LME crack sizes and types.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: New steel grades, in particular third-generation advanced high-strength steels, show a phenomenon called liquid metal embrittlement (LME), which is caused by a complex interplay of the applied zinc coating in combination with the heat and tensile stress resulting from the spot weld process [ 3 ,  4 ]. A susceptible base material is necessary to experience intergranular cracking by the liquid zinc [ 3 ]. Electrogalvanized zinc coatings (EG) are considered to lead to less LME cracking than hot-dip galvanized coatings [ 5 ]. For a given material, the LME cracking can be mitigated by changing the process parameters for manipulating the heat input or by adapting the boundary conditions, i.e., electrode caps [ 2 ,  6 ,  7 ,  8 ,  9 – 10 ]. The challenge in the serial production lies in the varying conditions due to wear, electrode alloying, manufacturing discontinuities and many other factors, which is why LME cracks cannot be ruled out for susceptible materials. Figure  1  shows a commonly used classification of LME cracks based on their location, with type A cracks being directly in the electrode indentation, type B cracks in the location of the electrode shoulders as well as the heat affected zone and type C cracks in the sheet-sheet interface [ 11 ]. According to guideline DVS 2960:2015-08 and DIN EN ISO 6520-2:2013-12, the crack locations lead to different effects on the static and fatigue strength of the joint [ 12 ,  13 ], but without correlation to the welded material, as no standard evaluation method exists for LME cracks. The guideline DVS 2960:2015-08 suggests that type A and type B cracks have no effect for static shear and fatigue load for crack depths of up to 33% of the sheet thickness, while type C cracks are not expected to have an effect on the shear fatigue life, independent of the crack length and depth. Fig. 1 LME crack classification [ 14 ], based on [ 11 ]

A wide range of research has investigated the influence of LME cracks on the mechanical properties of resistance spot welds. Depending on the material, test method, crack generation, crack size, as well as crack location, inconsistent findings have been made, which agree or contradict the guideline DVS 2960. Many researchers focused on the static shear and cross-tension strength. Wintjes et al. developed the crack index, which serves as a guideline for calculating the expected loss of quasistatic lap-shear strength due to LME based on the number of cracks per weld, the lognormal median crack length, and the sheet thickness [ 15 ]. Razmpoosh et al. collected different research and summarized the state of the art regarding the influence of the material combination in terms of their ultimate tensile strength (UTS) [ 3 ]. They showed that material combinations with high UTS > 1100 MPa tend to show a decrease in mechanical performance of more than 20%, corresponding to [ 16 ,  17 ,  18 ,  19 – 20 ]. Recent studies also found a significant influence of LME on the impact strength of specially designed S-rail components, which underscores the general relevance of investigating the effect of LME cracks for passenger safety [ 21 ,  22 ].

In terms of the impact of liquid metal embrittlement on fatigue life of resistance spot welds, researchers showed that no or minimal impact should be expected for type A and B cracks under lap-shear and cross-tension load [ 3 ,  17 ,  23 ,  24 ]. In contrast to that, research by Zou et al. showed a reduction of lap-shear fatigue life by nearly 50% under the influence of type B LME cracks, but with a comparatively small sample size of three welds and large deviations for crack-free samples [ 25 ]. The disparity of results is expected to arise from different testing conditions, crack types, materials, and other factors which have a significant impact on the fatigue life, as the test method is very sensitive to set boundary conditions [ 24 ,  26 ]. For example, manufacturing discontinuities like an angular misalignment have been used to not only provoke certain crack types but also influence the behavior during cyclic load [ 27 ,  28 ].

It can be summarized that the fatigue life of resistance spot welded AHSS remains a less understood topic, as the investigations are highly dependent on the set boundary conditions and hence the results are inconsistent. This results partly come from the fact that there exists no standardized procedure for evaluating the LME influence on fatigue life of resistance spot welds. A method for fatigue testing of resistance spot welds is described in the EN ISO 14324:2003-12 with tensile-shear and cross-tension specimen geometries, but without specifying the abort criterion, load ratio, or calculation of the S-N curve. Due to the inconsistency in the current literature, this study is aimed at developing a methodology for evaluating the LME influence on the S-N curve for single spot lap-shear specimens as per ISO 14324:2003-12 based on the fracture surface and digital image correlation (DIC), which can be transferred to different test conditions and specimen geometries.

sections.heading: Materials and welding equipment
paragraphs:
A 3G AHSS DP1220 HD with a sheet thickness of  t  = 1.4 mm and a microalloyed CR300LA, which is equal to a HX340LAD according to DIN EN 10346:2015-10, with a sheet thickness of  t  = 1.5 mm has been investigated. The DP1200 HD with a sheet thickness of  t  = 1.4 mm is generally considered LME susceptible in contrast to the CR300LA [ 29 ,  30 ]. Detailed chemical compositions, mechanical properties according to DIN 50125:2022-08 (geometry: DIN 50125-H 20 × 80), and information regarding the coating according to DIN EN 10346:2015-10 can be found in Table  1  [ 31 ,  32 ].
 Table 1 Chemical composition, mechanical properties, and coatings of investigated material Material Chemical composition [wt. %] Mechanical properties ( n  = 5) Coating per side ( n  = 5) C Si Mn Fe R p0.2  [Mpa] R m  [MPa] A 80  [%] DP1200 HD 0.2 1.5 2.5 Balanced 1022 ± 33 1239 ± 14 11.7 ± 0.3 Electrogalvanized 7.81 ± 0.27 µm CR300LA 0.06  < 0.01 0.31 Balanced 350 ± 1.1 438 ± 0.9 26.9 ± 0.4 Hot-dip galvanized 6.56 ± 0.04 µm

All welds have been performed on an electromagnetic C-frame spot weld system  (magneticDRIVE®, NIMAK GmbH).  The system allows for variable electrode forces during the weld time [ 33 ]. The welding current was generated with a 1 kHz MFDC inverter ( Bosch Rexroth AG ). Dome-shaped type F1-16–20-8–50-6 and truncated flat type B0-16–20–50-6–36 electrode tips made of CuCr1Zr alloy according to DIN EN ISO 5821:2025-10 have been used [ 34 ]. For all of the presented experiments, the upper and lower electrode tip geometry was equal.

sections.heading: Methodology for evaluating LME and fatigue cracks
paragraphs: Three types of LME cracks were distinguished as displayed in Fig.  1 . Further information can be found in [ 11 ,  14 ]. A distinction of type B cracks based on their location relative to the electrode shoulder, as proposed by Murugan et al. [ 38 ], has not been considered. In addition to that, the new crack type for short flanges found by Yang et al. [ 39 ], often referred to as type E, has not been detected for shown results and was therefore not included in this study. The focus of this study was put on type A and type B cracks. Figure  3  shows the steps used for evaluating the influence on LME cracks on the fatigue failure. Fig. 3 Methodology for evaluating the LME influence on fatigue life

The LME characterization done in step no. 3 served as a comparison for the fatigue life investigation, which was carried out in step no. 4 for different load levels together with the digital image correlation. Both experimental procedures will be explained in the following chapters in more detail. After the fatigue testing, another image was taken via a stereo microscope and compared to the image taken in step no. 3; in particular, the position of the fatigue crack and the LME crack length were noted so to determine the influence of cracks being present before the cyclic loading.
After the specimens were characterized, selected fracture surfaces were analyzed in the final step no. 6. For this, it was necessary to expose the LME crack surface without damaging it.

The specimen was first cut near the crack tip via wet cutting, where a clear coat was applied before to prevent the crack surface from being contaminated by the cooling water. A notch was added at the opposing side of the LME crack with a micro cutter. One side of the specimen was clamped afterwards and a uniaxial force was applied on the upper half, which led to the failure of the specimen in the desired location. A conventional tensile testing machine was used for that purpose for the displayed results. Finally, the clear coat was removed with acetone and the fracture surface analyzed with stereo and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The SEM analysis was carried out with a Zeiss Evo 15 ( Carl Zeiss AG ), which had an integrated EDX detector Zeiss SmartEDX ( Carl Zeiss AG ). A working distance of WD ≈ 10 mm was chosen as it has proven to yield the best results for the chosen system.

sections.heading: Methodology for generating LME cracks
paragraphs: Based on previous investigations, two parameter sets with a decreasing electrode force profile have been used and adapted for intentionally generating LME cracks. The heat input and tensile stresses are modified by this in comparison to conventional parameters. For more detailed information, please refer to [ 14 ]. The two parameter sets can be found in Table  2 , where the welding current is turned on during the force run-in, force decrease time and force run-out time. For DP1200 HD, a welding current of  I W  = 6.0 kA and for CR300LA a welding current of  I W  = 8.0 kA have been chosen, based on the WCR (cf. Fig.  2 ).

The repeatability of spot welds generated with the derived force profile was tested on ten consecutive welds with parameter set no. 1 (cf. Table  2  (a)) and F1-16–20-8–50-6 electrode tips for DP1200 HD (cf. Table  1 ). The electrode tips were dressed and alloyed beforehand with ten welds to minimize the alloying effect. Figure  4  shows three representative welds from the series. It is visible that for all welds, a type B LME crack at a similar location was achieved. Fig. 4 Surface view of representative welds for parameter set no. 1, welded with DP1200 HD and F1 electrode tips

For all welds, the electrode indentation, total crack length, and selected characteristic from the electrode displacement, based on [ 40 ], were analyzed to quantify the repeatability. The electrode displacement was measured via an absolute displacement sensor GT2-H12 ( Keyence Corp. ). The maximum electrode displacement resembles the maximum thermal expansion, and the total indentation displacement is the summed-up indentation displacement during the weld and hold time. Figure  5 a, b shows the related results and standard deviations. The electrode indentation in Fig.  5 a was measured optically with a 3D optical profilometer ( VR 6000, Keyence Corp. ). Both sides were measured, and the average between both was calculated. The total crack length was calculated by adding the length of all individual cracks for both sides, which were visible with 20x magnification. Fig. 5 a  Electrode indentation and crack length;  b  electrode displacement characteristic values for 10 consecutive welds with parameter set no. 1

It can be deduced that the resistance spot weld process with a decreasing electrode force is reproducible for the used welding machine. In addition to that, the LME cracks showed comparable types, locations, and sizes. The methodology for generating LME cracks was found suitable for investigating their influence on the mechanical properties.

sections.heading: Fatigue testing
paragraphs: The fatigue testing was carried out on a high-frequency pulsator “250 HFP 5100” ( ZwickRoell GmbH & Co. KG ) with a maximum force of 250 kN and a frequency range of 35–300 Hz. A hydraulic clamping “Hydrogrip 20 kN” ( Russenberger Prüfmaschinen AG ) was used with a clamping pressure of  p  ≈ 30 MPa. Due to the machine having no displacement sensor, the test procedure was solely controlled by the force and the specimen oscillated at the natural frequency, which was  f  ≈ 43 Hz in presented results. The abort criterion was, based on previous investigations, a frequency loss of  Δf  = 5 Hz or when  n  = 2×10 6  cycles was reached [ 23 ]. A frequency loss of  Δf  > 5 Hz leads to no significantly higher test cycles but to more damaged specimens, which hinders the fracture analysis. The frequency and force were internally recorded during the process and exported as a.csv file.

The tests were carried out and analyzed according to the national standard DIN 50100:2022-12. Three force amplitudes were investigated with the step method, based on prior experiments:  F 1  = 2.0 kN,  F 2  = 2.5 kN, and  F 3  = 3.0 kN with a load ratio of  R  = 0.1. As more than two force amplitudes were investigated, the string-of-pearls approach was used for the calculations according to the standard. Single spot specimens were used according to EN ISO 14324:2003-12, as shown in Fig.  6 . Fig. 6 Specimen geometry for fatigue testing according to EN ISO 14324:2003-12

sections.heading: Digital image correlation (DIC)
paragraphs: For the digital image correlation, a 2D system “Me-go Standard—5 M” ( Me-go GmbH ) has been used [ 41 ]. The camera has a resolution of 2.592 × 2.048 px with a sampling rate of up to 70 Hz. For the image acquisition, the software “GOM Snap 2D (2019)” was used. For illumination, a conventional ringlight has been installed and provided enough illumination. The camera had a distance of ≈ 19 cm to the workpiece. The analysis was made in “GOM Correlate (2019)”. The workpiece surface was primed with white spraypaint and a black stochastic pattern has been applied via spraying from a distance of ≈ 50 cm. The pattern quality was checked with the integrated software tool. As the used system does not provide the possibility to trigger via the force signal, a fixed frame rate of 1/30 Hz was used, which turned out to be sufficient for analyzing the crack propagation and elongation. The setup is shown in Fig.  7 . Fig. 7 DIC setup

sections.heading: LME crack characterization
paragraphs: The investigation of the crack surface serves as a reference for evaluating the influence on the fatigue life. The weld was prepared with the procedure described in chapter 2.4. The fracture surface for a selected weld with parameter set 1 (cf. Table  2  (a)) and a constant welding current of  I w  = 6.0 kA for DP1200HD can be seen in Fig.  8 c. The fracture surface can be separated into three regions, which correlate to findings made by Murugan et al. [ 42 ]. Fig. 8 LME crack surface for DP1200HD,  a  after welding,  b  after opening the crack, and  c  LME crack surface

A colorful heat tint is visible on the expected LME fracture surface in Fig.  8 c, which makes a clear distinction to the base material possible. A coarser microstructure is visible with progressing crack depth. Figure  9  shows the magnified fracture surface with three zones, based on the microstructure. Fig. 9 Magnified fracture surface for DP1200 HD with three different zones, based on the classification by [ 42 ]

It can also be seen that the maximum crack depth is not in the apex point of the crack as would have been expected. This shows that the conventional method of selecting the cutting plane does not necessarily lead to the measurement of the maximum crack depth in the cross-section.

Figure  10 a–c shows SEM images, taken with the SE detector, in different magnifications. Images taken with the BS detector did not provide better visibility of the fracture surface. Fig. 10 SEM images (SE) of the LME fracture surface;  a  detailed overview (100x);  b  detail of the transition area between zone 2 and 3 (310x);  c  detail of deposits on the LME crack surface (1500x)

Figure  10 b shows a magnification of the transition area between zones 2 and 3 (cf. Figure  9 ), where small deposits are visible under larger magnification in Fig.  10 c. EDX measurements showed that the mixed-element deposits contain up to 60% Zn, with the remaining elements matching the chemical composition of the base material (cf. Table  1 ). In addition to that, an EDX line-scan from the sheet surface in the direction of the crack tip and a mapping in zone 1 have been performed to investigate the distribution of zinc on the fracture surface. The results are displayed in Fig.  11 . Fig. 11 a  EDX line scan from the sheet surface ( x  = 0 µm) to the crack tip ( x  = 160 µm);  b  EDX mapping in zone 1 (cf. Figure  9 )

The observation indicates a decrease in zinc concentration with increasing crack depth. This phenomenon may be attributed to elevated temperatures resulting from nugget formation and reduced heat dissipation, which facilitate the evaporation of zinc. As illustrated in Fig.  11 b, Energy Dispersive X-ray (EDX) mapping identifies significant zinc infiltration in zone 1 (cf. Figure  9 ), accounting for an overall zinc content of 18% in the analyzed area. These findings corroborate the Liquid Metal Embrittlement (LME) crack mechanism associated with resistance spot welds manufactured under decreasing electrode force conditions. Moreover, they establish a baseline for comparative analysis against the fracture surfaces of fatigue-induced cracks in future works.

sections.heading: Digital image correlation (DIC)
paragraphs: In the following, the DIC will be shown for CR300LA (cf. Table  1 ) welded with B0-16–20–50-6–36 electrode tips, parameter set 2 (cf. Table  2  (b)) and  I w  = const. = 8.0 kA. Welds without zinc coating showed no visible cracking, so it is expected that the crack mechanism was based on liquid metal embrittlement. As the primary factor for the fatigue life of resistance spot welds is the weld geometry and not the base material strength, the results are expected to be transferable from CR300LA to DP1200 HD for similar nugget geometries and electrode indentations [ 43 ].

Figure  12 a shows a spot weld with severe LME cracking (crack length  l c  ≈ 9.6 mm), and Fig.  12 b the camera image of the weld surface after applying the speckle pattern with the used coordinate system. The crack depth was measured on separate cross sections and is expected to reach  d c  ≈ 1.5 mm, which equals the sheet thickness. Fig. 12 DIC of CR300LA:  a  overview after the welding process;  b  camera image after speckle pattern application with coordinate system

Figure  13  shows the change of frequency for the displayed spot weld with a force amplitude of  F a  = 3.0 kN and  R  = 0.1. The abort criterion of  Δf  = −5 Hz has been reached at  n  = 2.54×10 5  cycles. Fig. 13 Change of frequency during fatigue testing

As the cyclic loading was applied in y-direction (cf. Figure  12 ), the strain was calculated accordingly (cf. formula  3 ) and visualized in the software. The results are displayed in Fig.  14 . It can be seen that only the edges of the electrode contact areas and heat affected zones are affected by the mechanical load. Fig. 14 DIC for tensile fatigue test at different frequency levels

This corresponds with associated literature, where a potential influence of LME and heat affected zone (HAZ) cracks is only visible for cracks in specific locations [ 17 ,  18 ,  24 ,  25 ,  27 ,  28 ]. It is expected that the severe LME crack visible in Fig.  12 a had a negligible influence on the strain distribution. The potential of the digital image correlation for visualizing loaded areas and monitoring crack propagation during fatigue testing of resistance spot welds was confirmed. In future investigations, the presented method will be used to assist the quantification of a possible LME influence on the S-N curve by comparison of welds before and after fatigue testing.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: The fatigue life of resistance spot welds is affected by numerous factors, complicating the quantification of zinc-induced liquid metal embrittlement (LME) cracks’ impact on the S-N curve. This study developed a methodology to assess the influence of LME on cyclic loading behavior, consisting of the following steps: Reproducible LME crack generation is achieved by using a decreasing electrode force. The reproducibility was confirmed by analysis of crack type and length as well as the electrode indentation and electrode displacement for ten consecutive welds. The LME crack surface was exposed through precise cutting and separation of the specimen using movable clamping. Subsequently, the LME crack surface was analyzed using stereo microscopy and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to assess crack morphology. This analysis allows for comparison with the fracture surface following cyclic loading. Digital image correlation (DIC) was employed to monitor the fatigue test. The loaded areas are anticipated to vary under different testing conditions, such as specimen geometry, load direction, maximum load, stress ratio, and nugget geometry. To accurately quantify the influence of liquid metal embrittlement (LME) on the fatigue life of resistance spot welded structures, it is necessary to perform Digital Image Correlation for each specific case and critical condition.

Notably, in the case studied, a severe LME crack did not propagate under cyclic loading, indicating that crack location is the critical factor for the influence on fatigue life. The presented approach used a decreasing electrode force, which will be adapted in the second part of this investigation to generate different crack types and sizes. The impact of different LME cracks on the fatigue performance will be investigated and quantified for a specific case.
